title: Assign Cookies
approach_name: Sort and match smallest sufficient cookie
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Maximize satisfied children by matching each greed factor in g to a cookie size in s that is at least as large.
Idea: Sort both lists ascending; i tracks the least greedy unsatisfied child and j the current cookie. Advance i only when s[j]>=g[i], and always consume the cookie.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting plus two-pointer greedy assigns the smallest sufficient cookie first, preserving larger cookies for children who need them.
Invariant: After each consumed cookie, i counts children matched to distinct cookies, and all skipped cookies were too small for the current least greedy child.
Edge cases: Empty g or s returns zero; a cookie exactly equal to a greed factor satisfies that child; extra small cookies are skipped. Both input lists are sorted in place.
Complexity: O(n log n + m log m) time for sorting plus O(n+m) scan time, and O(1) explicit auxiliary space apart from sort internals.
time_complexity: O(n log n + m log m)
complexity_reason: The two lists are sorted, then pointers each move forward at most the length of their respective list.

title: Assign Cookies
approach_name: Sort and match smallest sufficient cookie
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of children whose greed factors can be met by distinct cookies of sufficient size.
Idea: Arrays.sort orders g and s; i points to the next unsatisfied child and j to the next cookie, which is always consumed after its suitability is checked.
Technique and why it applies: The smallest-sufficient-cookie greedy strategy avoids wasting a large cookie when a smaller one works.
Invariant: i is the number of children satisfied so far, and every cookie before j has been considered once.
Edge cases: Empty arrays yield zero; equal cookie and greed sizes count as a match; surplus small cookies cannot satisfy the current child. Arrays.sort mutates both arrays.
Complexity: O(n log n + m log m) time for sorting and O(n+m) for the scan, with O(1) explicit pointer storage.
time_complexity: O(n log n + m log m)
complexity_reason: Both arrays are sorted and the scan advances i and j monotonically, so each element is examined only a constant number of times.

title: 132 Pattern
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Detect indices i<j<k with nums[i]<nums[k]<nums[j], the 132 pattern.
Idea: Scan nums from right to left; stack holds possible middle values, and third stores the best popped candidate for the pattern's '2'. Return true when x<third.
Technique and why it applies: A reverse monotonic stack exposes a feasible middle value when a larger value is popped, avoiding a cubic search.
Invariant: third is a value already known to have a larger earlier-in-scan stack value above it, and any later x below third completes the pattern.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return false; [3,1,4,2] returns true; strictly increasing input has no 132 pattern. Python's negative-infinity sentinel is below ordinary integer values.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space because each value is pushed once and popped at most once.
complexity_reason: The reverse scan pushes and pops each number at most once, and the stack stores at most n values.

title: 132 Pattern
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Determine whether three ordered indices satisfy nums[i]<nums[k]<nums[j].
Idea: Scan from the final index backward; st stores candidates for the larger middle value, while third is updated from popped values and checked against each current number.
Technique and why it applies: The reverse monotonic stack keeps possible '3' and '2' values so a valid pattern can be detected without checking every triple.
Invariant: third is a popped value with a larger value encountered to its right, so a smaller current value proves the required ordering.
Edge cases: Fewer than three values cannot form the pattern; [3,1,4,2] returns true; strictly increasing data returns false. Long.MIN_VALUE provides a sentinel below every int, and stack entries are Integers.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) extra space because each array value is pushed once and popped at most once.
complexity_reason: The loop scans n elements and each element enters or leaves the deque at most once.

title: Circular Array Loop
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Detect a circular-array cycle of length greater than one whose jumps all have the same sign.
Idea: nxt rejects a direction change and one-element self-loop; each start uses slow and fast pointers. If they meet, a valid cycle exists; otherwise visited same-direction positions are zeroed.
Technique and why it applies: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare cycle detection finds a loop using pointers rather than a visited set, while direction checks enforce the problem's rule.
Invariant: During one start's pointer walk, slow advances one valid jump and fast advances two; any rejected jump ends that search before zero-marking the traversed direction chain.
Edge cases: A one-element loop is rejected; mixed-sign paths stop; an empty array returns false because the outer loop does not run. The code mutates nums by replacing explored values with zero.
Complexity: O(n) time overall and O(1) auxiliary space under the marking strategy, since failed paths are zeroed and each index is revisited only a bounded number of times.
code:
class Solution:
    def circularArrayLoop(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        n=len(nums)
        def nxt(i,direction):
            if nums[i]*direction<0:return -1
            j=(i+nums[i])%n
            return -1 if j==i else j
        for start in range(n):
            if nums[start]==0:continue
            direction=1 if nums[start]>0 else -1;slow=fast=start
            while True:
                slow=nxt(slow,direction)
                if slow==-1:break
                fast=nxt(fast,direction)
                if fast==-1:break
                fast=nxt(fast,direction)
                if fast==-1:break
                if slow==fast:return True
            cur=start
            while nums[cur]*direction>0:
                j=(cur+nums[cur])%n;nums[cur]=0;cur=j
        return False
complexity_reason: Each start uses constant pointers, and zero marking prevents the same directional chain from being fully explored repeatedly.

title: Circular Array Loop
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Determine whether circular jumps form a cycle longer than one with one consistent direction.
Idea: For each nonzero start, choose dir and run slow/fast through next; meeting proves a cycle. If not, zero out the same-direction path to avoid rechecking it.
Technique and why it applies: Floyd cycle detection uses constant-space pointers, while next enforces direction consistency and rejects self-loops.
Invariant: A pointer remains valid only while its jump sign matches dir and the computed next index differs from itself.
Edge cases: Empty input returns false; a self-loop is rejected; a direction-changing path terminates. The method mutates nums, and double-modulo normalization keeps negative jumps within array bounds.
Complexity: O(n) time overall and O(1) auxiliary space under path marking, because completed paths are set to zero and not explored again.
complexity_reason: The method keeps only indices and a direction flag, and zeroes traversed paths so each index receives bounded repeated work.

title: Repeated Substring Pattern
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Decide whether a nonempty string is formed by repeating a proper substring two or more times.
Idea: Concatenate s with itself, remove the first and last characters, and check whether the remaining string contains s.
Technique and why it applies: The doubled-string trick exposes a shifted occurrence exactly when s has a repeating block shorter than itself.
Invariant: A successful containment means a copy of s begins at a nonzero shift within the doubled string and ends before the original doubled boundary.
Edge cases: A one-character string returns false; 'abab' returns true; 'aba' returns false. The statement assumes nonempty input, and containment is a substring check rather than a character-set check.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the doubled string and sliced substring, with substring search linear in typical implementations.
complexity_reason: The code builds a doubled string and a length-2n-2 slice, then performs a substring search.

title: Repeated Substring Pattern
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Determine whether a nonempty string can be constructed by repeating a proper substring.
Idea: Build doubled=s+s, remove its first and last characters with substring, then test whether that interior contains s.
Technique and why it applies: The doubled-string property turns repetition detection into a substring search without trying every possible block length.
Invariant: If s is periodic with a shorter block, a shifted copy appears wholly inside the trimmed doubled string; a primitive string does not.
Edge cases: A one-character string returns false; 'abab' returns true; 'aba' returns false. Java substring indices are valid for the stated nonempty input, and doubled length is proportional to s.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for doubled, the substring, and the containment search.
complexity_reason: The method allocates strings proportional to n and searches the trimmed doubled string once.

title: Hamming Distance
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Return the number of bit positions at which nonnegative integers x and y differ.
Idea: Compute x^y, which sets bits wherever the operands differ, then return the number of set bits with bit_count().
Technique and why it applies: XOR isolates differing bit positions, and population count totals those positions directly.
Invariant: Every set bit in x^y corresponds to exactly one position where x and y have different bits.
Edge cases: Equal inputs return zero; 1 and 4 differ in two positions; high bits are counted as well. The usual problem domain is nonnegative integers.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space for fixed-width integer inputs; bit_count processes the XOR result's bits.
complexity_reason: The method performs one XOR and one population-count operation without allocating input-sized data structures.

title: Hamming Distance
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Count bit positions where integer values x and y differ.
Idea: XOR x and y, then pass the result to Integer.bitCount to count all set bits.
Technique and why it applies: XOR produces a one exactly at positions where the operands disagree, making population count the required Hamming distance.
Invariant: The result counts the set bits of x^y, each representing one differing bit position.
Edge cases: Equal inputs return zero; 1 and 4 differ at two positions; Java bit operations use the int bit pattern, including its sign bit for negative values.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) extra space for int inputs because the method calls a fixed-width bit-count operation.
complexity_reason: The implementation uses one XOR and one Integer.bitCount call with no loops or collections.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements II
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Minimize the sum of absolute changes needed to make every array value equal; the input must be nonempty.
Idea: Sort nums, choose nums[len(nums)//2] as the median, and sum abs(x-mid) for every element.
Technique and why it applies: The median minimizes total absolute distance, so choosing it avoids evaluating every possible target value.
Invariant: After sorting, the chosen middle value has at least half the observations on each side, balancing the total movement cost.
Edge cases: A singleton returns zero; [1,2,3] costs 2; negative values are handled by abs. Empty input fails when indexing the median, and sorting mutates nums.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting plus O(n) summation and O(1) extra space apart from sorting internals.
complexity_reason: Sorting dominates at O(n log n), then one pass sums distances to the selected median.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements II
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Find the minimum sum of absolute increments or decrements needed to make all array entries equal.
Idea: Sort nums, select nums[nums.length/2] as median, accumulate long absolute differences, and cast the total to int.
Technique and why it applies: The median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations, allowing the optimal target to be selected after sorting.
Invariant: The chosen middle element balances values below and above it, which minimizes total distance to a common target.
Edge cases: A singleton costs zero; [1,2,3] costs 2; negative values work with Math.abs((long)x-median). Empty input is outside constraints, and the final int cast can overflow if the total exceeds int range.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting plus O(n) summation and O(1) explicit extra space.
complexity_reason: Arrays.sort orders n values, and the following loop calculates one long difference per element.

title: Island Perimeter
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Compute the perimeter of a single island in a binary grid by counting land edges exposed to water or outside.
Idea: For each land cell add four; subtract two when its upper neighbor is land and two when its left neighbor is land, counting shared edges only once.
Technique and why it applies: Counting four sides per land cell and removing shared edges avoids checking every direction separately.
Invariant: Each adjacency is subtracted once when the later cell in row-major order sees its upper or left land neighbor.
Edge cases: A single land cell has perimeter 4; two horizontally adjacent land cells have perimeter 6; water cells contribute nothing. The implementation assumes a rectangular grid.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(1) extra space because every grid cell is inspected with constant neighbor checks.
complexity_reason: The nested loops inspect each of the m*n cells and perform at most two adjacency checks for land.

title: Island Perimeter
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Return the perimeter of one island in a rectangular grid where 1 denotes land and 0 denotes water.
Idea: For each land cell add four sides, then subtract two for an upper land neighbor and two for a left land neighbor.
Technique and why it applies: Shared-edge subtraction counts each land-water boundary without double-counting land-to-land edges.
Invariant: The perimeter variable equals the exposed edge count for all cells processed in row-major order.
Edge cases: One land cell gives 4; two adjacent horizontal cells give 6; water cells add nothing. The code reads grid[0].length, so an empty outer array is not supported.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(1) extra space because each cell gets constant-time checks and only perimeter is accumulated.
complexity_reason: The nested loops visit every grid position once and check only its upper and left neighbors.

title: Can I Win
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Decide whether the first player can force a win by taking unused numbers 1..maxChoosableInteger until the total reaches desiredTotal.
Idea: Return true if desiredTotal<=0 and false if the sum of all choices is too small; otherwise memoized win(mask,remaining) tries each unused bit and wins if a pick reaches the target or leaves the opponent losing.
Technique and why it applies: Bitmask game DP represents used numbers compactly, and memoization avoids re-solving identical remaining-choice states.
Invariant: For a given mask, the set of used numbers and their sum are fixed, so the remaining target and outcome are determined by that state.
Edge cases: A nonpositive target returns true; an unattainable target returns false; a move equal to remaining wins immediately. The cached recursion can be exponential in maxChoosableInteger, so the bitmask bound matters.
Complexity: O(2^M * M) time and O(2^M) memo space for M=maxChoosableInteger, since each mask tries up to M choices.
complexity_reason: The cache stores outcomes by mask and each state scans at most M candidate integers.

title: Can I Win
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player can force a win when players alternate choosing unused values from 1 through maxChoosableInteger.
Idea: Handle nonpositive targets and insufficient total sum first; then memo[mask] stores win(mask,remain), which tries each unused bit and returns true if a move reaches remain or forces a losing reply.
Technique and why it applies: Bitmask dynamic programming encodes the chosen set in an integer, and memoization shares results among identical masks.
Invariant: The chosen mask determines the remaining available numbers and cumulative sum, so each mask has a consistent win/loss result.
Edge cases: A nonpositive target returns true; if all numbers sum below target the method returns false; choosing x>=remain wins immediately. Java allocates 1<<max memo entries and relies on the problem's small maximum for safe bitmask size.
Complexity: O(2^M * M) time and O(2^M) space for the Boolean memo array and recursion, where M is the maximum choice.
complexity_reason: Each reachable mask is memoized once and its win method scans at most M possible picks.

title: Unique Substrings in Wraparound String
approach_name: Longest valid suffix per ending letter
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Count distinct nonempty substrings of p that occur in the infinite wraparound alphabet string.
Idea: Track the current consecutive wraparound run; for each ending letter update best[letter] with the longest valid run ending there, then sum best.
Technique and why it applies: A longest run ending in a letter represents every shorter wraparound substring ending at that letter, so only the maximum length per ending letter is needed.
Invariant: best[c] never decreases and stores the greatest valid wraparound suffix length observed for character c.
Edge cases: Empty p returns zero; 'zab' forms a length-three wraparound run; a break such as 'azc' resets the run when adjacent letters do not advance cyclically. The code assumes lowercase English letters.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space because it scans p once and keeps 26 counters.
complexity_reason: The scan updates one of 26 entries per character and the final sum visits the fixed-size array.

title: Unique Substrings in Wraparound String
approach_name: Longest valid suffix per ending letter
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Count distinct nonempty substrings of p that appear in the cyclic alphabet sequence.
Idea: For each character, extend run when its difference from the previous character is one modulo 26; otherwise reset to one, update best[x], and sum all entries.
Technique and why it applies: For each ending letter, a maximum valid suffix length accounts for all shorter wraparound substrings ending at that letter.
Invariant: best[x] stores the longest cyclic-consecutive substring ending in character x seen anywhere in the scan.
Edge cases: Empty p returns zero; 'zab' produces a run of three; a nonconsecutive transition resets run. Character indexing assumes lowercase a-z, and modulo 26 handles z-to-a wraparound.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space for one scan and a 26-element array.
complexity_reason: Each character updates one fixed-array slot and the final loop sums 26 values.

title: Validate IP Address
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Classify queryIP as IPv4, IPv6, or Neither using exact component counts and each protocol's component syntax.
Idea: Three dots select IPv4 parsing: split into four parts, reject empty, non-digit, leading-zero, or >255 components. Seven colons select IPv6 parsing and require eight 1-4 digit hexadecimal groups.
Technique and why it applies: Component-by-component validation checks syntax and bounds rather than relying on permissive address parsers.
Invariant: The method returns a protocol label only after every component passes its format checks; an incorrect delimiter count or invalid component returns Neither.
Edge cases: '1.2.3.4' is IPv4; '01.2.3.4' is rejected for a leading zero; eight valid hex groups form IPv6. Python isdigit accepts some non-ASCII digits, so unusual Unicode numerals may pass the IPv4 digit check if int also accepts them.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for splitting the input into components, where n is queryIP length.
complexity_reason: Delimiter checks and splits scan queryIP, and the IPv4 and IPv6 loops inspect each component character at most once.

title: Validate IP Address
notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Classify an address string as IPv4, IPv6, or Neither using strict component counts, lengths, and character ranges.
Idea: Count dots or colons to select a format; split with a negative limit to preserve trailing empty components, then validate four decimal IPv4 parts or eight hexadecimal IPv6 groups.
Technique and why it applies: Explicit component validation enforces protocol-specific syntax without accepting compressed IPv6 or permissive numeric formats.
Invariant: The method returns IPv4 or IPv6 only after every expected component passes, and malformed delimiters or characters cause an immediate Neither result.
Edge cases: '1.2.3.4' is IPv4; '01.2.3.4' is rejected; trailing dots remain empty parts because split uses -1. IPv4 accumulation stays small for validated digit lengths, and character checks restrict digits to ASCII.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for component arrays and character scans, where n is the input length.
complexity_reason: Delimiter counting, splitting, and component scans each process at most the input's characters.
